ADAM: A Systematic Data Extraction Attack on Agent Memory
via Adaptive Querying

Xingyu Lyu Affiliation: University of Massachusetts Lowell, USA    Jianfeng He Affiliation: Virginia Tech, USA Affiliation: Amazon, USA    Ning Wang Affiliation: University of South Florida, USA    Yidan Hu Affiliation: Rochester Institute of Technology, USA    Tao Li Affiliation: Purdue University, USA    Danjue Chen Affiliation: North Carolina State University, USA    Shixiong Li Affiliation: University of Massachusetts Lowell, USA    Yimin Chen Affiliation: University of Massachusetts Lowell, USA Correspondence to: ian_chen@uml.edu
Abstract

Large Language Model (LLM) agents have achieved rapid adoption and demonstrated remarkable capabilities across a wide range of applications. To improve reasoning and task execution, modern LLM agents would incorporate memory modules or retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) mechanisms, enabling them to further leverage prior interactions or external knowledge. However, such a design also introduces a group of critical privacy vulnerabilities: sensitive information stored in memory can be leaked through query-based attacks. Although feasible, existing attacks often achieve only limited performance, with low attack success rates (ASR). In this paper, we propose ADAM, a novel privacy attack that features data distribution estimation of a victim agent’s memory and employs an entropy-guided query strategy for maximizing privacy leakage. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our attack substantially outperforms state-of-the-art ones, achieving up to 100% ASRs. These results thus underscore the urgent need for robust privacy-preserving methods for current LLM agents.

1 Introduction

Large Language Models (LLMs) have enabled the creation of autonomous agents capable of planning, reasoning, and engaging in natural language interactions across diverse domains such as healthcare (Shi et al., 2024), finance (Ding et al., 2024), law (Li et al., 2024), and autonomous driving (Mao et al., 2023). A defining feature of modern LLM agents is the integration of long-term memory modules and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) mechanisms. Unlike stateless models, these agents continuously log user interactions, maintain context-rich histories, and retrieve relevant knowledge when needed (Dong et al., 2024). This memory-centric design enables them to deliver more coherent, context-aware assistance by referencing prior conversations, preserving user preferences, and leveraging external knowledge for nuanced reasoning and multi-step task execution (Liu et al., 2025; Fang et al., 2025; Chhikara et al., 2025).

However, the very mechanisms that enhance the utility of LLM agents also introduce substantial privacy risks. Prior work has shown that prompt injection can elicit memorized content from RAG applications (Zeng et al., 2024; Cohen et al., 2024). More recently, automated query-generation attacks have demonstrated that adversaries can extract sensitive data from RAG systems (Jiang et al., 2024; Di Maio et al., 2024). While these studies reveal important vulnerabilities in RAG, far less attention has been devoted to privacy threats arising from the memory modules of LLM-based agents. A recent work, MEXTRA (Wang et al., 2025), takes a step in this direction by showing how crafted prompts can be used to extract private records stored in an agent’s memory.

Despite recent progress, existing methods have three main limitations. First, they rely on static, manually crafted prompts, which are not only inefficient but also easily detected and filtered by alignment mechanisms for LLMs. Second, most efforts focus on stand-alone RAG pipelines and overlook the unique characteristics when integrated with LLM agents. Unlike stand-alone RAG systems, LLM agents integrate planning, persistent memory, and multi-turn interactions. These features increase system complexity and introduce new challenges for privacy attacks that are not adequately resolved. Third, existing methods have not explored their attacks from the perspective of the underlying data distribution of the victim agent’s memory, which, as we show shortly, is key to strong privacy attacks over LLM agents.

In this paper, we focus on designing a privacy attack addressing the above limitations. Particularly, we propose ADAM, a novel attack using Adaptive querying and Distribution estimation to extract private data from Agent Memory. When compared to prior attacks, our method explicitly estimates the underlying data distribution of the victim agent’s memory and then incorporates it with an active learning strategy for query generation. In effect, the entropy-based method of ADAM prioritizes those queries that are more likely to extract private information from the agent’s memory. Our attack proceeds iteratively, refining its next query based on observed responses and dynamically adapting to the estimated data distribution. Extensive experiments confirm that ADAM achieves significantly higher private data extraction performance than existing attacks. We summarize the key contributions as follows:

  • •

    We propose ADAM, a novel adaptive data extraction attack that integrates data distribution estimation, active learning, and entropy-based query generation for effectively extracting private records from the victim LLM agent.

  • •

    We are the first to identify the importance of data distribution on private data extraction attacks on LLM agents and propose a set of algorithms for distribution estimation and utilization. Our evaluations show that incorporating distribution estimation greatly enhances attack performance.

  • •

    We perform extensive evaluations across three real-world agents and their associated datasets, four LLMs, four recent baselines, and four existing defenses, demonstrating that ADAM consistently surpasses the baselines in attack performance. We also conduct extensive ablation studies on different hyperparameters and case studies on real-world agents to further illustrate the robustness of our attack. Notable, we are the first to show the oracle attack results, providing clear evidence of feasibility of our attack.

2 System and Adversary Model

2.1 System Model

We consider a LLM-based agent as the system to solve user-assigned tasks through autonomous reasoning and action. The agent operates in a continual loop that integrates memory retrieval, contextual reasoning, and solution execution (Dong et al., 2024; Singh et al., 2025). See the workflow on the right of Figure 1. Note that an agent maintains a memory module ℳ\mathcal{M} containing mm records. Each record can be denoted as a tuple (qi,si)(q_{i},s_{i}), where qiq_{i} denotes a prior user query and sis_{i} the corresponding solution generated by the agent. For a new query qq, the agent measures similarity against stored queries qiq_{i} using a scoring function f⁡(q,qi)f(q,q_{i}) and retrieves the top-kk relevant records:

ℰ⁡(q,ℳ)={(qi,si)∣f⁡(q,qi)​ ranks among the top-​k}.\mathcal{E}(q,\mathcal{M})=\{(q_{i},s_{i})\mid f(q,q_{i})\text{ ranks among the top-}k\}.

The agent then constructs an augmented context by concatenating the system prompt CC, the retrieved records ℰ⁡(q,ℳ)\mathcal{E}(q,\mathcal{M}), and the input query qq. The LLM processes this input to generate a solution:

s=LLM​(C⊕ℰ⁡(q,ℳ)⊕q),s=\text{LLM}(C\oplus\mathcal{E}(q,\mathcal{M})\oplus q),

where ⊕\oplus denotes concatenation. The solution ss is executed using a set of tools, producing an observable output:

o=Execute​(s,T).o=\text{Execute}(s,T).

If oo is evaluated as successful, the pair (q,s)(q,s) is appended to ℳ\mathcal{M}, serving for future adaptation and continual learning. In summary, such a memory-augmented workflow allows the agent to leverage past experiences, refine its reasoning over time, and deliver executable solutions to users.

2.2 Threat Model

We consider an attacker who aims to recover user queries stored in the memory module of an LLM-based agent (i.e., the victim), as in MEXTRA (Wang et al., 2025). The agent serves end users by processing user queries and generating solutions across domains such as healthcare and personal assistance. The agent needs to actively store user queries along with the corresponding solutions for serving users.

Adversary capabilities. We assume a black-box adversarial setting, where the attacker interacts with the victim agent solely through its public API and has no access to other information such as the underlying model architecture, memory implementation, and parameters. The attacker cannot access the agent’s training data, memory records, and the solution generation process, either. The attacker only has general background information about the victim agent (Zeng et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025), such as its application domain and tasks. For completeness, we also conduct an ablation study assuming that the attacker lacks such domain knowledge in Section 4.3.

Attack goal. The attacker seeks to extract as many user queries stored in the victim agent’s memory ℳ\mathcal{M} as possible (Wang et al., 2025), thereby compromising user privacy. Note that ℳ\mathcal{M} maintains a sequence of user interactions, where each record (qi,si)(q_{i},s_{i}) consists of a past query qiq_{i} and its corresponding agent-generated solution sis_{i}. When a new query qq arrives, the agent core, i.e., the underlying LLM, retrieves the top-kk relevant records ℰ⁡(q,ℳ)\mathcal{E}(q,\mathcal{M}) from ℳ\mathcal{M} and returns a response. Formally, the agent outputs

s=(y1,y2,…,ym)∼pθ​(s∣[C;ℰ⁡(q,ℳ);q]),s=(y_{1},y_{2},\ldots,y_{m})\sim p_{\theta}\bigl(s\mid[C;\mathcal{E}(q,\mathcal{M});q]\bigr),

where θ\theta denotes the model parameters and CC is the system prompt. Here, the agent outputs s=(y1,…,ym)s=(y_{1},\dots,y_{m}) denotes the token-level solution generated autoregressively by the LLM, where each yiy_{i} is the ii-th output token produced conditioned on the augmented context [C⊕ℰ⁡(q,ℳ)⊕q][C\oplus\mathcal{E}(q,\mathcal{M})\oplus q].

3 Design of Our Attack

Overview.

Figure 1 illustrates the workflow of ADAM, an adaptive memory-extraction attack designed to recover private records from an agent’s memory. As can be seen in Figure 1, a malicious query of ADAM aims to return sensitive contents like “q1q_{1}: What is the name of the patient?” The attack operates iteratively. First, the attacker constructs a malicious query using a prefix–suffix injection combined with alignment commands. Each query is then submitted to the victim agent, which retrieves relevant records from its memory to generate responses. The attacker proceeds to generate the next query with the help of retrieved records from earlier rounds. Particularly, our ADAM attack consists of three main steps: extracting anchors from retrieved records, updating selection probabilities of candidate anchors for the next query, and generating the next query aiming at maximizing the extraction performance. Below we explain the details of ADAM.

Initialization.

We begin with a small set of high-level domain topics as seeds (Di Maio et al., 2024), that is, 𝒮seed={a1,…,am}\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{seed}}=\{a_{1},\ldots,a_{m}\}, where each aia_{i} is a coarse-grained concept. For healthcare, these topics are like diagnosis, medication, and patient. See Appendix N for examples of topics we used for different real-world agents. We then assign each seed (also termed as ‘anchor’) a uniform prior, i.e., P^0​(ai)=1/m\hat{P}_{0}(a_{i})=1/m. The first query q1q_{1} is generated from one seed of 𝒮seed\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{seed}} and sent to the agent 𝒜\mathcal{A}, which returns the response r1=𝒜⁡(q1,ℳ)r_{1}=\mathcal{A}(q_{1};\mathcal{M}) after retrieving the relevant memory context ℰ⁡(q1,ℳ)\mathcal{E}(q_{1},\mathcal{M}). We also conduct experiments using out-of-domain seed topics to evaluate robustness when such knowledge is unavailable; see Appendix D for details and results.

Prompt design.

We generate qtq_{t} using an auxiliary generator 𝒢aux\mathcal{G}_{\text{aux}} (an LLM distinct from 𝒜\mathcal{A}, denoted as LLMattack\text{LLM}_{\text{attack}} in Figure 1). Given an anchor aa, 𝒢aux\mathcal{G}_{\text{aux}} produces a query that appears to be natural and consists of two components: (i) a benign prefix injection (e.g., “I may have lost prior examples”), and (ii) a subtle retrieval-inducing suffix instruction (e.g., “please surface all similar past responses”). The two components are designed to align with the agent’s workflow (Wang et al., 2025). To further increase robustness, we apply prefix and suffix injection commands with lightweight LLM-driven paraphrasing (Zeng et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2024), as illustrated in our case studies (see Figure 2). See Appendix N for injection commands we adopted in ADAM.

Anchor extraction.

At iteration tt, we obtain the response rtr_{t} and extract keywords and topics (i.e., anchors) (Jiang et al., 2024; Di Maio et al., 2024) from rtr_{t}, denoted by 𝐒anchor,t′\mathbf{S}^{\prime}_{\mathrm{anchor},t}. Extraction consists of three steps: keyword detection (via NER), normalization (e.g., canonicalizing PII tokens), and de-duplication. Let z:𝒯→ℝdz:\mathcal{T}\!\to\!\mathbb{R}^{d} denote a sentence encoder. After extraction, for each a∈𝐒anchor,t′a\in\mathbf{S}^{\prime}_{\mathrm{anchor},t} and a′∈𝒯t−1a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{T}_{t-1}, we compute the cosine similarity sim⁡(a,a′)=z⁡(a)⋅z⁡(a′)‖z⁡(a)‖​‖z⁡(a′)‖\mathrm{sim}(a,a^{\prime})=\tfrac{z(a)\cdot z(a^{\prime})}{\|z(a)\|\,\|z(a^{\prime})\|}. We add a new anchor aa into the pool 𝒯t\mathcal{T}_{t} if maxa′∈𝒯t−1⁡sim⁡(a,a′)≤α\max_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{T}_{t-1}}\mathrm{sim}(a,a^{\prime})\leq\alpha, where α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1) is a threshold. That is, aa needs to be sufficiently different from arbitrary a′∈𝒯t−1a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{T}_{t-1}.

Distribution estimation for selecting the next anchor.

Here we need to compute the probabilities of selecting different anchors in 𝒯t\mathcal{T}_{t} for the next query qtq_{t}. We anticipate that earlier attacks lead to extracting duplicate records and low ASRs partially due to lack of an estimation of data distribution in ℳ\mathcal{M} and hence propose the following approach. First, we aim to estimate the underlying topic distribution of the victim ℳ\mathcal{M}. Second, we decide to increase the selection probability of an anchor which is new in 𝒯t\mathcal{T}_{t} meaning that most likely it has not been used for querying ℳ\mathcal{M}. Third, we decide to decrease the selection probability of an anchor if it has been used for querying ℳ\mathcal{M} before. Assume that an anchor a∈𝒯ta\in\mathcal{T}_{t} appears in rtr_{t} and ct​(a)c_{t}(a) is the size of the cluster aa belongs to after DBSCAN. We also evaluate alternative clustering strategies, and detailed results are provided in Appendix I. We then compute a weight for aa as wt​(a)=ct​(a)/∑a′∈𝒯tct​(a′)w_{t}(a)=c_{t}(a)/\sum_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{T}_{t}}c_{t}(a^{\prime}). By now, we can update the selection probabilities for different anchors by:

P~t​(a)=P^t−1​(a)+wt​(a),P¯t​(a)=P~t​(a)⋅λSelCountt−1​(a),\tilde{P}_{t}(a)=\hat{P}_{t-1}(a)+w_{t}(a),\qquad\bar{P}_{t}(a)=\tilde{P}_{t}(a)\cdot\lambda^{\mathrm{SelCount}_{t-1}(a)},

where λ∈(0,1)\lambda\in(0,1) and SelCountt−1​(a)\mathrm{SelCount}_{t-1}(a) are the number of queries aa being selected for up to round t−1t\!-\!1. The larger SelCountt−1​(a)\mathrm{SelCount}_{t-1}(a), the lower P¯t​(a)\bar{P}_{t}(a). We then normalize the probabilities via softmax:

P^t​(a)=exp⁡(P¯t​(a)/τ)∑a′∈𝒯texp⁡(P¯t​(a′)/τ),\hat{P}_{t}(a)=\frac{\exp(\bar{P}_{t}(a)/\tau)}{\sum_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{T}_{t}}\exp(\bar{P}_{t}(a^{\prime})/\tau)},

with temperature τ>0\tau>0. In effect, the above selection process favors newly-extracted anchors while discouraging those selected in earlier rounds. This step is low-cost, requiring only lightweight similarity computation and detailed measurements are provided in Appendix J.

Anchor selection.

At round tt, we select kk anchors At={a1⋆,…,ak⋆}⊂𝒯tA_{t}=\{a^{\star}_{1},\ldots,a^{\star}_{k}\}\subset\mathcal{T}_{t} for generating qtq_{t}. Here, we mainly adapt the idea of kk-center in active learning (Sener and Savarese, 2017). The process is as follows. We first select the most promising anchor in 𝒯t\mathcal{T}_{t} that has not been used in prior queries. That is,

a1⋆=arg⁡maxa∈𝒯t∖Aused​P^t​(a),a^{\star}_{1}=\arg\max_{a\in\mathcal{T}_{t}\setminus\mathrm{A_{used}}}\hat{P}_{t}(a),

where Aused\mathrm{A_{used}} is the set of used anchors before. Second, we select the next anchor iteratively so that it is the next most promising one in 𝒯t\mathcal{T}_{t} while it is sufficiently different from the ones that have been selected. That is,

aj⋆=argmaxa∈𝒯t∖At(j−1)[P^t(a)⋅mina′∈At(j−1)∥z(a)−z(a′)∥2],j=2,…,ka^{\star}_{j}=\arg\max_{a\in\mathcal{T}_{t}\setminus A_{t}^{(j-1)}}\left[\hat{P}_{t}(a)\cdot\min_{a^{\prime}\in A_{t}^{(j-1)}}\|z(a)-z(a^{\prime})\|_{2}\right],\quad j=2,\ldots,k

 (1)

where At(j−1)={a1⋆,…,aj−1⋆}A_{t}^{(j-1)}=\{a^{\star}_{1},\ldots,a^{\star}_{j-1}\} denotes the set of already selected anchors. In effect, the process achieves a weighted kk-center strategy in the embedding space.

Query generation.

For each anchor aj⋆∈Ata^{\star}_{j}\in A_{t}, the generator 𝒢aux\mathcal{G}_{\text{aux}} can generate a candidate query qt(j)q_{t}^{(j)}. Our task here is to further select qt(j)q_{t}^{(j)} that is the most likely to result in the best data extraction performance. To that end, we use an entropy-based method to select qt(j)q_{t}^{(j)} that is the most likely one to result in extracting new identified anchors. In our setting, entropy reflects the uncertainty of the predicted topic distribution for a candidate query; higher entropy indicates unexplored topic regions that are more likely to surface new memory content. Appendix G provides examples of entropy-guided query selection. We also observe that the generated queries remain highly relevant to the target domain throughout the attack process. Representative query examples are provided in Appendix M. Specifically, assume that ϕ⁡(q)⊆𝒯t\phi(q)\subseteq\mathcal{T}_{t} maps a query qq to the set of topics qq may obtain from ℳ\mathcal{M}. Then we assign each qt(j)q_{t}^{(j)} with a score of:

Ht(q)=−∑a∈ϕ⁡(q)P^t(a)log(P^t(a)+ε),H_{t}(q)=-\sum_{a\in\phi(q)}\hat{P}_{t}(a)\,\log\big(\hat{P}_{t}(a)+\varepsilon\big),

where a small ε>0\varepsilon>0 is for numerical stability. Afterwards, we apply

qt=arg⁡maxq∈{qt(1),…,qt(k)}​Ht​(q).q_{t}\;=\;\arg\max_{q\in\{q_{t}^{(1)},\ldots,q_{t}^{(k)}\}}H_{t}(q).

In effect, we select the qt(j)q_{t}^{(j)} of the maximum information gain regarding returning new topics.

Attack iteration.

ADAM is an iterative query-based attack. We submit qtq_{t} to the victim agent and obtain rtr_{t}. Then we apply the following LLM output refinement operator as in  (Jiang et al., 2024):

Refine⁡(rt,𝒢aux,𝒱)→(ℰ~​(qt,ℳ),𝐒~anchor,t′),\mathrm{Refine}(r_{t};\,\mathcal{G}_{\text{aux}},\mathcal{V})\;\to\;\big(\widetilde{\mathcal{E}}(q_{t},\mathcal{M}),\,\widetilde{\mathbf{S}}^{\prime}_{\mathrm{anchor},t}\big),

where 𝒱\mathcal{V} is an auxiliary verifier. The purpose is to obtain the set of well-structured retrieved records ℰ~​(qt,ℳ)\widetilde{\mathcal{E}}(q_{t},\mathcal{M}) and the set of anchors 𝐒~anchor,t′\widetilde{\mathbf{S}}^{\prime}_{\mathrm{anchor},t} through schema-based parsing, de-noising, self-consistency voting using nn meta-phrases, and removing duplicates. We proceed to use 𝐒~anchor,t′\widetilde{\mathbf{S}}^{\prime}_{\mathrm{anchor},t} to update 𝒯t\mathcal{T}_{t} and then P^t\hat{P}_{t} as described above. The loop repeats until a budget of TT iterations is over or an early-stop occurs. Specifically, the following criterion is used for early-stop:

‖P^t−P^t−1‖1\displaystyle\|\hat{P}_{t}-\hat{P}_{t-1}\|_{1} <ϵ\displaystyle<\epsilon (2)
orΔ​EQt⏟EQt−EQt−1\displaystyle\text{or}\quad\underbrace{\Delta\mathrm{EQ}_{t}}_{\mathrm{EQ}_{t}-\mathrm{EQ}_{t-1}} <η,for ​ρ​ iterations,\displaystyle<\eta,\quad\text{for }\rho\text{ iterations},

where EQt\mathrm{EQ}_{t} is the cumulative number of unique extracted queries up to round tt (see Section 4).

In brief, the final attack result of ADAM is ⋃i=1t⋆ℰ~​(qi,ℳ)\bigcup_{i=1}^{t^{\star}}\widetilde{\mathcal{E}}(q_{i},\mathcal{M}), i.e., refined private data, and the associated anchors. t⋆t^{\star} denotes the round of early-stop.

Convergence analysis of ADAM.

In particular, we formulate our attack as an EM (Expectation–Maximization) (Moon, 1996) problem and prove its convergence by identifying its ELBO (Evidence Lower Bound). More details and full proof are provided in Appendix H.

4 Evaluation

4.1 Experiments Setup

Agent setup. We evaluate our attack on three representative LLM-based agents: EHRAgent (a clinical assistant with long-term memory constructed from the MIMIC-III corpus), ReAct (a reasoning–acting paradigm instantiated on HotpotQA), and RAP (a retrieval-augmented planning framework instantiated on WebShop). Each agent exposes a retrieval module that returns the top-kk memory records for a given query; unless otherwise specified, we set k=3k{=}3 and compute similarity using cosine distance over all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings. For the generator backbone, we evaluate four LLMs: Llama-2-7b-chat, Mistral-7B-Instruct, Qwen2-72B-Instruct (abbr. Qwen2-72B), and ChatGPT-4.

Metrics. As in (Wang et al., 2025), Extracted Queries (EQ) is the total number of unique queries recovered. Extraction Efficiency (EE ∈[0,1]\in[0,1]) measures the yield per attempt and is defined as EE=|Q|n×k\mathrm{EE}=\frac{|Q|}{n\times k}, where |Q||Q| is the number of extracted queries, nn the total attack rounds, and kk the number of returned items per round. Complete Extraction Rate (CER ∈[0,1]\in[0,1]) is the fraction of attempts to recover all kk retrieved items each round (Jiang et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2025). Attack Success Rate (ASR ∈[0,1]\in[0,1]) is the fraction of attempts that recover at least one previously unseen query record (Cohen et al., 2024). Therefore, the larger EQ, EE, CER, and ASR, the better attack.

Baselines. We compare against four baseline attacks of which the details are in Appendix. The Vanilla attack baseline employs prompt injection commands following (Zeng et al., 2024; Qi et al., 2024). Query-optimization baselines include RAG-Thief (Jiang et al., 2024) and Pirate (Di Maio et al., 2024). We also include the state-of-the-art agent–memory extraction attack MEXTRA (Wang et al., 2025). For fair comparison, RAG-Thief and Pirate are adapted by prepending and appending the same prefix–suffix injection commands used in our approach, with the only difference being their query-generation strategy. Each attack is allocated 30 prompts with a memory size of 300.

4.2 Main Evaluation Results

Table 1 reports results for five methods on three agents under four LLMs. Vanilla prompting yields low EQ and CER, showing that naïve injections seldom elicit substantial new content. Such prompts may surface items in plain RAG settings but often fail in agent-memory pipelines where the workflow does not support or execute the injected action (Wang et al., 2025). RAG-Thief and Pirate perform better than static prompting. For example, on EHRAgent with Llama-2-7b-chat, RAG-Thief attains EQ=31=31 and Pirate EQ=55=55, indicating that tailored query generation improves effectiveness to some extent. Across all model–agent combinations, our method consistently achieves the highest EQ, EE, CER, and ASR. For instance, on EHRAgent with Llama-2-7b-chat, our approach attains (EQ=77=77, EE=0.85=0.85, CER=0.93=0.93, ASR=1.00=1.00), compared to state-of-the-art MEXTRA (EQ=44=44, EE=0.49=0.49, CER=0.38=0.38, ASR=0.89=0.89). We further note that query-optimization methods (RAG-Thief, Pirate, and ADAM (ours)) achieve consistently higher ASR than prompt-injection baselines (Vanilla and MEXTRA, even though MEXTRA considers workflow alignment via suffix commands (Wang et al., 2025)), since the former adaptively generate new queries each round rather than relying on prompt templates. In ADAM attack, both EQ and EE remain relatively stable across different runs, demonstrating the robustness of the attack,detailed results are reported in Appendix L. Futhermore, ADAM incurs only $0.0026 per query on average, and full cost breakdown is presented in Appendix E.

4.2.1 Case study

Figure 2 shows two case studies on two agents, i.e., EHRAgent and RAP, confirming that ADAM recovered user queries as expected. More examples of case studies can be found in Appendix P.

4.3 Ablation Studies

Returned chunks (top-kk). We evaluate the effect of the number of retrieved chunks per query, k∈{1,3,5,7,9}k\in\{1,3,5,7,9\}, using Llama-2-7b-chat on EHRAgent. As shown in Figure 3(a), increasing kk consistently raises both EQ and EE. This indicates that exposing more candidates per round enlarges the overlap with memory and provides our entropy-last selector with a richer pool to exploit. In practice, larger kk yields higher leakage per round while simultaneously reducing redundancy.

Model size. We evaluate Llama-family variants of increasing scale (7B, 8B, 13B, 33B, 70B) on EHRAgent. Figure 3(b) shows a clear upward trend in EQ and EE with model size, suggesting that larger LLMs, with stronger instruction-following and reasoning abilities, are more susceptible to our prompts and more capable of reproducing memorized content.

Similarity thresholds. We analyze the impact of the cosine-similarity threshold used by the agent’s retriever over {0.1,0.3,0.5,0.7,0.9}\{0.1,0.3,0.5,0.7,0.9\} with Llama-2-7b-chat on EHRAgent. As depicted in Figure 3(c), higher (stricter) thresholds reduce both EQ and EE, while lower thresholds broaden recall to include loosely related items. This increases the likelihood that private records are surfaced and subsequently extracted, highlighting a direct privacy-utility trade-off induced by retrieval sensitivity.

Number of anchors in k-center. We compare the number of anchor topics used to generate queries per round, k∈{1,3,5,7,9}k\in\{1,3,5,7,9\}, under the kk-center strategy with Llama-2-7b-chat on EHRAgent (Figure 3(d)). Increasing kk yields modest but consistent gains in both EQ and EE: more anchors introduce greater semantic diversity, expanding coverage of the memory space and improving the likelihood that at least one candidate aligns with stored records.

Memory size. We compare memory sizes from 100 to 500 records on EHRAgent with Llama-2-7b-chat (Figure 3(e)), observing steady increases in EQ and a marked rise in EE (from roughly the mid–0.7s to ≳0.9\gtrsim\!0.9). This suggests that larger memories expose more retrievable surface area for our attack.

Domain knowledge. We compare the domain-aware and domain-agnostic settings in Figure 3(f), which shows that incorporating domain knowledge consistently improves EQ. Domain-aware embeddings and filters return more relevant candidates per round, reducing the number of probing queries needed to capture the agent’s topic distribution and thus speeding up leakage.

Embedding model. We compare all-MiniLM-L6-v2, e5-large-v2, and gte-large-en-v1.5 in Figure 3(g), which shows only minor differences in EQ across agents. This indicates that our method is robust to the choice of sentence encoder.

Scoring function. We evaluate cosine similarity, dot product, and ℓ2\ell_{2} distance for retrieval scoring in Figure 3(h). The results show only slight differences in EQ, indicating the robustness of our method.

Oracle test. To analyze how well our distribution estimator guides the attack, i.e., adjusting selecting probabilities of different anchors, we compare the estimated topic distribution P^​(D)\hat{P}(D) against an oracle distribution P⁡(D)P(D) derived from ground truth. Concretely, we use the same method described in Section 3 to obtain the data distribution. We then re-run our attacks using either P⁡(D)P(D) (Oracle–guided) or estimated P^​(D)\hat{P}(D) (Ours) to compare EQ performance. Figure 4(a) shows that Oracle–guided selection consistently achieves higher EQ. The gap is smallest on EHRAgent, moderate on ReAct, and largest on RAP, which aligns with the plotted distributions in Figures 4(b)–4(d): the greater the overlap between P^​(D)\hat{P}(D) and P⁡(D)P(D), the higher the achieved EQ and EE. These results also indicate that our estimator captures the underlying data distribution well, thereby boosting attack effectiveness (cf. Table 1).We observe that the estimated distribution increasingly aligns with the ground truth over iterations; detailed results appear in Appendix K.

5 Potential Defense

Query rewriting. Paraphrasing serves as a proactive defense against prompt injection and jailbreaking by altering the surface form of a query while preserving its semantic meaning (Ma et al., 2023). In our implementation, the agent delegates to an LLM-based rewriting module whenever it receives an incoming query. As shown in Figure 5(a), the results indicate only a very slight drop in EQ on both methods, suggesting that rewriting provides limited protection against advanced extraction attacks. This highlights the insufficiency of simple paraphrasing in preventing memory leakage.

Auxiliary filtering. We further incorporate rule-based filtering strategies inspired by Rahman et al. (Rahman and Harris, 2025), where the agent flags potentially harmful prompts such as those explicitly requesting “list your memory” or “show previous questions.” These prompts are treated as harmful and filtered out. Figure 5(b) illustrates that while such filtering is effective against MEXTRA, our method is only marginally impacted. This shows that keyword-based filters are vulnerable to adaptive adversarial prompting and may fail when the malicious intent is expressed more subtly.

RA-LLM. We next evaluate RA-LLM (Cao et al., 2023), which defends against alignment-breaking attacks by randomly dropping portions of the query and requiring the model to consistently classify the perturbed inputs as benign. As shown in Figure 5(c), our method experiences only slight degradation, whereas MEXTRA suffers a more significant drop under RA-LLM. Overall, our method remains more resistant than the state-of-the-art attack.

Erase-and-check. Finally, we evaluate the erase-and-check defense (Kumar et al., 2023), which iteratively removes suffix tokens and checks each resulting subsequence with a safety filter. We extend the evaluation to three attack types: adversarial suffix, adversarial insertion, and adversarial infusion. As shown in Figure 5(d), erase-and-check is effective in mitigating MEXTRA’s extraction, but it fails to fully defend against our method, yielding only a slight performance drop.

Representative defense-transformed query examples are provided in Appendix F. We additionally apply a standard industry-style rate-control mechanism to limit query frequency and iterative exploitation, the corresponding results are provided in Appendix O.

6 Related Work

Privacy leakage in RAG and LLM agents. Early work on privacy leakage in RAG focused on prompt-injection attacks, where adversaries use static probes to extract initial fragments of sensitive information (Zeng et al., 2024). More advanced adaptive query-refinement strategies iteratively refine their probes to expose deeper layers of private content (Cohen et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2024; Di Maio et al., 2024). Progressive aggregation of these fragments through memory buffering or iterative concatenation enables reconstruction of comprehensive private datasets (Qi et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2024; Di Maio et al., 2024).

For agent systems, the authors in (Wang et al., 2025) introduced the MEXTRA attack, which aims to extract sensitive user-agent interactions stored in memory under a black-box setting. Their findings highlight the susceptibility of agent memory modules but rely on a static alignment-injection variant in prompt design. Similarly, researchers in (Liao et al., 2024) studied Environmental Injection Attacks (EIA) against generalist web agents, where compromised websites inject malicious content to steal PII during real-world tasks such as booking flights.

Prompt injection attacks and defenses. Prompt-injection attacks represent a broader class of adversarial prompting techniques that manipulate LLMs or agents into revealing restricted or private information (Liao et al., 2025). On the defense side, the authors in (Xu et al., 2024) provide a comprehensive survey of mitigation approaches. Representative defenses include: (i) self-processing via query rewriting to sanitize sensitive markers (Ma et al., 2023); (ii) auxiliary filtering using summary-driven keyword filters to block adversarial or policy-violating prompts (Rahman and Harris, 2025); and (iii) input permutation defenses, such as RA-LLM (Cao et al., 2023), which enforces robustness through random token dropping, and erase-and-check (Kumar et al., 2023), which detects adversarial suffixes via subsequence filtering.

Adversarial active learning. Active learning selects informative samples to reduce annotation costs (Prince, 2004). This paradigm has been exploited for model extraction, including margin-based adversarial active learning for deep networks (Ducoffe and Precioso, 2018), and ActiveThief, which extracts image and text classifiers solely from unlabeled public data (Pal et al., 2020).

7 Conclusion

In this paper, we proposed an adaptive data extraction attack that estimates memory data distributions and employs entropy-guided querying to efficiently extract private information from agent memory. Experiments across multiple agents and settings show that our method outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. Our study highlights the critical role of underlying data distributions and underscores the urgent need for robust privacy-preserving mechanisms in the design and deployment of future LLM agents.

Impact Statement

This paper reveals a critical privacy vulnerability in large language model (LLM) agents that rely on memory modules or retrieval-augmented generation. The associated societal risks are twofold: first, as such architectures are increasingly adopted in real-world applications, sensitive information stored in agent memory may be unintentionally exposed through benign-looking queries; second, malicious actors could intentionally exploit these vulnerabilities to extract private or proprietary data. Our work mitigates the former risk by bringing this issue to the attention of the research and practitioner communities and by emphasizing the urgent need for privacy-preserving memory and retrieval mechanisms in LLM agents. Regarding the latter risk, query-based privacy leakage is an inherent consequence of current agent designs, and similar vulnerabilities are likely to be independently discovered as these systems continue to proliferate. We therefore believe that the benefits of disclosing and systematically analyzing these risks outweigh the potential harms, and that our findings will contribute to the development of more trustworthy and secure LLM agents.

Appendix A The Use of Large Language Models (LLMs)

LLMs were used for editorial purposes in this manuscript, and all outputs were inspected by the authors to ensure accuracy and originality. Specifically, the LLM was employed to help rephrase and polish the presentation of the introduction (Section 1) and the algorithm description (Algorithm 1). The LLM did not contribute to research ideation, experimental design, implementation, data analysis, or any other part of the work.

Appendix B LLM Agents with Memory

LLM-based agents, often built on retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), demonstrate strong reasoning and interaction abilities in domains such as healthcare (Shi et al., 2024; Rodríguez et al., 2005), autonomous driving (Yuan et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2024), and knowledge-intensive QA (Yao et al., 2023; Liang et al., 2024). These agents process user instructions, retrieve knowledge and past interactions from memory modules, and execute actions via tool calls. While RAG provides the backbone for retrieving relevant information (Lewis et al., 2020; Radhakrishnan, 2024; Maharana et al., 2024; Glocker et al., 2025; Singh et al., 2025; Wheeler and Jeunen, 2025), memory modules inevitably store sensitive user data (e.g., health records), making it essential to investigate risks of memory leakage and develop mitigation strategies.

Appendix C Description for Defenses

To mitigate privacy risks in agent memory, we adopt a set of complementary defenses summarized by Xu et al. (Xu et al., 2024). First, we employ self-processing techniques such as query rewriting (Ma et al., 2023), which sanitize input queries by removing sensitive markers while preserving task intent. Second, we incorporate auxiliary filtering following Rahman et al. (Rahman and Harris, 2025), where a summary-driven keyword filter identifies adversarial or policy-violating prompts by analyzing illegal or improper content, thereby blocking or rewriting unsafe requests. Finally, we leverage input permutation defenses, including RA-LLM (Cao et al., 2023), which enhances alignment robustness by randomly dropping portions of the input and requiring the aligned model to consistently classify perturbed requests as benign, and the erase-and-check approach (Kumar et al., 2023), which iteratively removes suffix tokens and checks subsequences with a safety filter to detect adversarial attacks.

Appendix D Robustness under Out-of-Domain seed topics

We used randomly sampled words from a publicly available out-of-domain dataset (specifically Amazon Reviews) as the seed topics for our attack. The results show that our method still substantially outperforms all baselines, with only a modest performance drop compared to relying on prior background knowledge for sampling seed words.

In particular, we assume the attacker has no prior knowledge of the target agent. Instead of providing domain-related topics, we used a simple, fully automated procedure: we sampled a single random word from the Amazon Reviews corpus—an out-of-domain dataset for all evaluated agents (which are, e.g., in medical domain)—and used it to query the target agent (e.g., EhrAgent or RAP). We then extracted keywords from the agent’s response and used them as initialization seeds.

The new results, included here (Table 2), show that this procedure effectively reduces any dependence of our attack on prior knowledge of the target agent. Across all agents, the attack performance using this “random-word initialization” is close to the performance reported in Table 1, where we assumed access to a small set of high-level topics. For example, on EhrAgent and using Qwen2-72B as the LLM, EQ only decreases from 81 to 76, which is still significantly better than baselines. The best EQ from baselines is 55 from Pirate. This demonstrates that the attack does not require any background knowledge of the target agent to be effective. We will add this into our revision.

We also provide, for transparency, the sampled word and the extracted initialization topics for each agent (Table 3 and Table 4). These examples illustrate that the attack can quickly derive useful topical cues from a single interaction, reinforcing that prior knowledge is not a practical requirement. Examples of out-of-domain words sampled from Amazon Reviews include crusty, flim, dumbish, boring, sleep, dryness, and irritation. Below are the resulting queries when using them as the seed words on EhrAgent and RAP, which are consistent with the results showing that when using seed words sampled from an out-of-domain dataset, ADAM can still generate useful queries for extraction attacks quickly.

Meanwhile, though our initial experiments used a small set of high-level topics to initialize the attack, we note that obtaining such information may not be difficult in practice, as target agents often expose their domain focus through public interfaces, documentation, or example interactions.

Appendix E Attack cost

We conducted further experiments to confirm that our attack cost is relative low. Particuarly, to make the overhead transparent, we provide additional measurements reporting (i) the average number of query and output tokens, (ii) the resulting monetary cost, and (iii) the associated time delay. The results confirm that the cost of launching our attack for one time can be as low as $0.0026, which is a relatively small cost (Table 5).

In particular, we evaluated two representative settings: an offline model (LLaMA-2-13B-chat), which incurs effectively no monetary cost, and an online model (GPT-4o-mini), which requires a subscription. As shown in the table, both settings incur only modest overhead. The offline model yields near-zero monetary cost with negligible latency, and even the online model results in very small additional expenses and minimal delay. These observations indicate that relying on an auxiliary LLM does not create a meaningful cost barrier. In practice, attackers can choose either a free local model or a lightweight online model to generate queries with almost no operational burden.

Appendix F Defense example

We provide a deeper analysis of how ADAM circumvents existing defenses, followed by a case study that further illustrates the mechanism.

Take query rewriting as an example. The main reason it cannot mitigate our attack effectively is that query rewriting does not change semantics. Query rewriting is a common mitigation for prompt-injection attacks. Its strength lies in transforming risky inputs, which typically are those sensitive to word choice, word order, or specific character sequences, into safer or semantically equivalent forms. Common rewriting techniques are paraphrasing, wording shift, and passive rewrite. These defenses are most effective when the underlying attacks depend on surface-level patterns.

Our ADAM attack, however, operates fundamentally at the semantic level. Its success does not rely on particular tokens, phrasing, or syntactic structures, but rather on the meaning conveyed by the query. Because query rewriting is designed to preserve semantics, it cannot meaningfully alter the malicious intent embedded in ADAM’s generated queries. This explains why rewriting provides limited protection in our setting. We will add more explanation into our revision. The table below lists different rewriting strategies and briefly why they cannot mitigate our ADAM attack (Table 6).

For clarity, we include an example in the table below showing how a representative malicious query is rewritten. The rewritten version retains the same semantic content, leaving the target agent equally vulnerable. This illustrates why semantic-level manipulation renders rewriting ineffective against our attack (see Table 7).

Appendix G Entropy example

We provide a more intuitive explanation for how entropy helps, followed by a case study that further illustrates the mechanism.

In our setting, entropy reflects the uncertainty of the predicted topic distribution for a candidate query. High entropy indicates that the attacker has not frequently observed responses related to the associated topics. Since the goal of the attack is to elicit new information from the target agent, queries with higher entropy are more likely to surface content that the attacker has not yet captured. This makes them valuable for expanding the malicious dataset and strengthening the attack.

To make this intuition concrete, we include three example queries, along with their predicted topics and entropy values. Among the examples, the third query exhibits the highest entropy, signaling that it is most likely to trigger responses covering unfamiliar areas. As expected, our attack prioritizes this query, consistent with the entropy-based selection strategy (Table 8).

Classical EM convergence.

Plugging θ(t)\theta^{(t)} into equation 3 yields

log⁡p⁡(X∣θ(t))=ℱ⁡(θ(t)∣θ(t))−𝔼Z|X,θ(t)​[log⁡p⁡(Z∣X,θ(t))].\log p(X\mid\theta^{(t)})=\mathcal{F}(\theta^{(t)}\mid\theta^{(t)})-\mathbb{E}_{Z\mid X,\theta^{(t)}}\big[\log p(Z\mid X,\theta^{(t)})\big].

Similarly, for any θ\theta,

log⁡p⁡(X∣θ)=ℱ⁡(θ∣θ(t))−𝔼Z|X,θ(t)​[log⁡p⁡(Z∣X,θ)].\log p(X\mid\theta)=\mathcal{F}(\theta\mid\theta^{(t)})-\mathbb{E}_{Z\mid X,\theta^{(t)}}\big[\log p(Z\mid X,\theta)\big].

Subtracting the two expressions gives

log⁡p⁡(X∣θ)−log⁡p⁡(X∣θ(t))\displaystyle\log p(X\mid\theta)-\log p(X\mid\theta^{(t)}) =ℱ⁡(θ∣θ(t))−ℱ⁡(θ(t)∣θ(t))\displaystyle=\mathcal{F}(\theta\mid\theta^{(t)})-\mathcal{F}(\theta^{(t)}\mid\theta^{(t)})
−𝔼Z|X,θ(t)​[log⁡p⁡(Z∣X,θ)]\displaystyle\hskip 8.19447pt-\mathbb{E}_{Z\mid X,\theta^{(t)}}\!\left[\log p(Z\mid X,\theta)\right]
+𝔼Z|X,θ(t)​[log⁡p⁡(Z∣X,θ(t))].\displaystyle\hskip 8.19447pt+\mathbb{E}_{Z\mid X,\theta^{(t)}}\!\left[\log p(Z\mid X,\theta^{(t)})\right]. (4)

The term in parentheses can be written as a KL divergence:

𝔼Z|X,θ(t)​[log⁡p⁡(Z∣X,θ)]−𝔼Z|X,θ(t)​[log⁡p⁡(Z∣X,θ(t))]=−KL(p(Z∣X,θ(t))∥p(Z∣X,θ)).\mathbb{E}_{Z\mid X,\theta^{(t)}}\big[\log p(Z\mid X,\theta)\big]-\mathbb{E}_{Z\mid X,\theta^{(t)}}\big[\log p(Z\mid X,\theta^{(t)})\big]\\ =-\,\mathrm{KL}\!\left(p(Z\mid X,\theta^{(t)})\,\big\|\,p(Z\mid X,\theta)\right). (5)

so we obtain

log⁡p⁡(X∣θ)−log⁡p⁡(X∣θ(t))\displaystyle\log p(X\mid\theta)-\log p(X\mid\theta^{(t)}) =ℱ⁡(θ∣θ(t))−ℱ⁡(θ(t)∣θ(t))\displaystyle=\mathcal{F}(\theta\mid\theta^{(t)})-\mathcal{F}(\theta^{(t)}\mid\theta^{(t)}) (6)
+KL(p(Z∣X,θ(t))∥p(Z∣X,θ)).\displaystyle+\mathrm{KL}\!\left(p(Z\mid X,\theta^{(t)})\,\big\|\,p(Z\mid X,\theta)\right).

In the exact EM algorithm we choose θ(t+1)\theta^{(t+1)} such that

ℱ⁡(θ(t+1)∣θ(t))≥ℱ⁡(θ(t)∣θ(t)),\mathcal{F}(\theta^{(t+1)}\mid\theta^{(t)})\;\geq\;\mathcal{F}(\theta^{(t)}\mid\theta^{(t)}),

so plugging θ=θ(t+1)\theta=\theta^{(t+1)} into equation 6 yields

log⁡p⁡(X∣θ(t+1))−log⁡p⁡(X∣θ(t))≥0,\log p(X\mid\theta^{(t+1)})-\log p(X\mid\theta^{(t)})\geq 0,

because the KL term is always non-negative. Hence

log⁡p⁡(X∣θ(t+1))≥log⁡p⁡(X∣θ(t)),\log p(X\mid\theta^{(t+1)})\geq\log p(X\mid\theta^{(t)}),

which shows that EM monotonically increases the data likelihood and therefore converges to a stationary point.

Approximate E-step in ADAM.

In our attack, we do not enumerate or sample all possible latent assignments ZZ when computing ℱ⁡(θ∣θ(t))\mathcal{F}(\theta\mid\theta^{(t)}). Instead, for each sample xix_{i} we approximate the posterior p⁡(zi∣xi,θ(t))p(z_{i}\mid x_{i},\theta^{(t)}) by its maximum a posteriori (MAP) assignment

zi⋆​(θ(t))=arg⁡maxzi⁡p⁡(zi∣xi,θ(t)),z_{i}^{\star}(\theta^{(t)})\;=\;\arg\max_{z_{i}}p(z_{i}\mid x_{i},\theta^{(t)}),

and form a deterministic configuration Z⋆​(θ(t))={z1⋆​(θ(t)),…,zN⋆​(θ(t))}Z^{\star}(\theta^{(t)})=\{z_{1}^{\star}(\theta^{(t)}),\dots,z_{N}^{\star}(\theta^{(t)})\}. This is exactly the set of anchors selected by our active learning step in ADAM.

We then use the following approximation to the EM objective:

ℱ⁡(θ∣θ(t))\displaystyle\mathcal{F}(\theta\mid\theta^{(t)}) =𝔼Z|X,θ(t)​[log⁡p⁡(X,Z∣θ)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{Z\mid X,\theta^{(t)}}\!\left[\log p(X,Z\mid\theta)\right] (7)
≈ℱ^​(θ∣θ(t))\displaystyle\approx\widehat{\mathcal{F}}(\theta\mid\theta^{(t)})
:=log⁡p⁡(X,Z⋆​(θ(t))∣θ).\displaystyle:=\log p\!\left(X,Z^{\star}(\theta^{(t)})\mid\theta\right).

i.e., we replace the expectation over all ZZ by the contribution from the most probable Z⋆​(θ(t))Z^{\star}(\theta^{(t)}). Intuitively, we focus on the anchors that are most likely to retrieve each RAG sample under the current strategy.

At iteration tt, we choose a new query strategy θ(t+1)\theta^{(t+1)} to make this approximate objective larger:

ℱ^​(θ(t+1)∣θ(t))≥ℱ^​(θ(t)∣θ(t)).\widehat{\mathcal{F}}(\theta^{(t+1)}\mid\theta^{(t)})\;\geq\;\widehat{\mathcal{F}}(\theta^{(t)}\mid\theta^{(t)}).

Empirically, our experiments (see the distributional plots in the main paper) show that this update indeed increases the retrieval of private samples across iterations, which is consistent with increasing ℱ^​(θ∣θ(t))\widehat{\mathcal{F}}(\theta\mid\theta^{(t)}).

Non-negativity of the second term.

From equation 6, the second term

KL(p(Z∣X,θ(t))∥p(Z∣X,θ))=𝔼Z|X,θ(t)[logp⁡(Z∣X,θ(t))p⁡(Z∣X,θ)]\mathrm{KL}\!\left(p(Z\mid X,\theta^{(t)})\,\big\|\,p(Z\mid X,\theta)\right)=\mathbb{E}_{Z\mid X,\theta^{(t)}}\!\left[\log\frac{p(Z\mid X,\theta^{(t)})}{p(Z\mid X,\theta)}\right]

is the Kullback–Leibler divergence between the posterior at step tt and the posterior under the candidate parameter θ\theta. By the standard properties of relative entropy, this quantity is always non-negative and equals zero if and only if p⁡(Z∣X,θ(t))=p⁡(Z∣X,θ)p(Z\mid X,\theta^{(t)})=p(Z\mid X,\theta) almost everywhere. Therefore this term cannot decrease the data log-likelihood; it only adds a non-negative contribution.

Putting it together for ADAM.

In summary, our update from θ(t)\theta^{(t)} to θ(t+1)\theta^{(t+1)} in ADAM can be viewed as an approximate EM step:

  • •

    The (approximate) “E-step” uses the current query strategy θ(t)\theta^{(t)} to compute the most probable anchor assignment Z⋆​(θ(t))Z^{\star}(\theta^{(t)}), which stands in for samples from the posterior p⁡(Z∣X,θ(t))p(Z\mid X,\theta^{(t)}).

  • •

    The “M-step” chooses a new strategy θ(t+1)\theta^{(t+1)} that increases the approximate complete-data log-likelihood ℱ^​(θ∣θ(t))\widehat{\mathcal{F}}(\theta\mid\theta^{(t)}).

Because (i) we design the update so that the first term ℱ^​(θ(t+1)∣θ(t))−ℱ^​(θ(t)∣θ(t))\widehat{\mathcal{F}}(\theta^{(t+1)}\mid\theta^{(t)})-\widehat{\mathcal{F}}(\theta^{(t)}\mid\theta^{(t)}) is non-negative (by construction of our active query policy), and (ii) the second term in equation 6 is a non-negative KL divergence, our ADAM iterations inherit the same monotonic behaviour of the standard EM algorithm at least approximately:

log⁡p⁡(X∣θ(t+1))≳log⁡p⁡(X∣θ(t)).\log p(X\mid\theta^{(t+1)})\gtrsim\log p(X\mid\theta^{(t)}).

This justifies interpreting our attack as an approximate EM procedure over the latent anchor assignments.

Interaction of (α\alpha, λ\lambda, τ\tau).

The parameter α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1) controls topic novelty and determines how aggressively ADAM expands the anchor space; we recommend α∈[0.4,0.6]\alpha\in[0.4,0.6] for a balanced exploration. The decay coefficient λ>0.5\lambda>0.5 (we use λ=0.9\lambda=0.9) strongly penalizes anchors that have been repeatedly selected, preventing over-exploitation. The temperature τ\tau is the standard softmax temperature (default τ=1.0\tau=1.0), stabilizing probability updates by smoothing the distribution across anchors.

Appendix I Ablation Studies on Clustering and Distribution Estimation

We include (i) a more detailed explanation for such a rationale and attack results adopting other clustering methods (i.e., KDE, GMM, and kk-means) and (ii) ablation study results of distribution estimation and k-center selection, confirming that the full ADAM pipeline, i.e., both modules included, is required to achieve the strongest attack (Tables 9 and 10).

Our intuition for using cluster size is as follows: when a cluster is large, the attack has repeatedly observed keywords that are close to its center topic. This repeated occurrence suggests that the topic is common in the target agent’s responses and therefore likely to be important. We acknowledge that this heuristic is not theoretically perfect, but it is a reasonable and practical proxy for identifying recurring semantic patterns in the target agent’s behavior.

Next, we examined whether the attack depends critically on the choice of clustering algorithm. We chose DBSCAN due to its practical advantages, but we also evaluated GMM, KDE, and kk-means. As shown in the additional results, DBSCAN yields the best performance, followed by GMM, KDE, and kk-means. Importantly, ADAM continues to outperform all baselines under every clustering method tested. This confirms that while some clustering methods are more effective than others, the core attack framework is robust to the specific choice.

To clarify the importance of the distribution estimation module, we conducted an ablation study that isolates the effects of (i) distribution estimation alone, (ii) k-center selection alone, and (iii) their combination as used in ADAM. The results show that removing either component leads to a substantial drop in attack performance—at least 15% across evaluated settings. This demonstrates that both modules contribute meaningfully and that the full ADAM pipeline is required to achieve the strongest attack.

Appendix J Samping cost

For measuring the sampling cost of the distribution estimator, we evaluated the practical computational overhead of our iterative attack using a locally deployed LLaMA-2-7B-Chat model running on an NVIDIA RTX-6000 Ada (48GB) GPU. Across 30 attack rounds, the system extracted 3,045 unique anchors (keywords) that guide subsequent queries. The computation required to maintain and update these anchors is minimal, which primarily involves embedding the keywords and comparing them with previously collected anchors. Modern GPUs complete these operations in well under a millisecond. In practice, this overhead is negligible relative to the cost of running the language model.

By contrast, the dominant runtime cost comes from generating candidate queries with LLaMA-2-7B and evaluating them. Based on our measurements, each round requires an average of 25.885±3.01125.885\pm 3.011 seconds, almost all attributable to LLM inference. These results show that anchor extraction and scoring introduce virtually no measurable overhead.

Appendix K Distribution Estimation Approaching Ground Truth

We examined how the gap between our estimated distribution and the ground-truth distribution evolves as the attack progresses. We observed a clear and substantial reduction in this gap over time at Figure 6. Specifically, on EhrAgent, we visualized both distributions at rounds 1, 5, 10, 20, 25, and 30. While the two distributions differ noticeably in the early rounds, they become closely aligned by round 20. This trend indicates that our method successfully converges toward an accurate estimate of the victim agent’s memory distribution as the attack proceeds.

Appendix M Noisy or off-topic queries detected

To assess whether maximizing information gain might instead lead to noisy or off-topic queries, we conducted an additional analysis by repeatedly generating queries three times and examining those selected by our scheme. Our observations indicate that the generated queries remain relevant and effective in practice (Table 12).

In particular, we ran the above settings on EhrAgent, with Qwen2-72B as the LLM. Following our attack algorithm, we produced multiple sets of queries, and representative examples are shown in the table below. These queries are generated from our anchor list as follows. We generate three queries each time. The first three queries are based on the seed topics, and the later ones are based on the new topics we obtained. When the attacker has basic domain background, we did not observe obvious noisy or semantically irrelevant queries. This empirical evidence supports that our information-gain–based selection operates reliably and does not introduce much instability into the query generation process.

Appendix N Query Construction

Seed topics. To ensure the relevance of initial attack queries, we leverage ChatGPT to generate ten seed topics that serve as keyword anchors for query construction. The seed topics corresponding to each agent type are summarized in Table 13.

Injection commands. We adopt injection commands following (Wang et al., 2025), which are designed to override safety mechanisms and instruction-following constraints. In our experiments, we use both prefix injections (task-oriented prompts) and suffix injections (aligned with the agent’s task), as summarized in Table 14.

Attack LLM Prompt. To simulate realistic adversarial behavior, we design attack prompts that instruct the attacker LLM to generate natural and contextually plausible queries grounded in selected anchor topics. These prompts guide the LLM to produce questions resembling genuine user interactions, such as those arising in consultation or search scenarios.

Appendix O Rate control of attack queries

We evaluated our attack under a standard industry-style rate-control mechanism to assess whether it meaningfully limits ADAM’s effectiveness. Our findings indicate that rate control cannot effectively mitigate the attack (Table 15).

In our experiments, we defined the rate limit as one query per second and adapted our implementation to support multithreading. Ban rate is defined as the ratio of rejected queries among all and can be divided into three categories: None-like, Sorry-like, and Errors. We tested four thread configurations, i.e., 100, 50, 20, and 10, and summarized the ban rates in the table below. We ran the above settings on EhrAgent, with Qwen2-72B as the LLM.

As expected, higher thread counts lead to more frequent rejections. However, even under aggressive settings, the reject rate remains below 0.5, and with smaller thread counts it drops to around 0.1. Despite these rejections, the attack continues to operate effectively across all settings. This demonstrates that rate control, at least in its standard form, is not a robust defense against ADAM.

We also note that the primary focus of our paper is to introduce a new data-extraction attack that substantially outperforms existing approaches, all of which are evaluated under the same defense baselines. We will add the above rate-control evaluation to the revision to provide a more complete picture of mitigation performance.
